Continue reading...

Geopolitics.title: Ukraine-Russia talks: What are the US objectives?
Geopolitics.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday in their first official visit to Ukraine as part of a renewed push for peace, more than 4½ years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. We discuss this topic with our guest, John E. Herbst, director of the Eurasia Center at the Atlantic Council.

Geopolitics.title: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner hold Ukraine talks after meeting Putin
Geopolitics.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv, seeking to revive efforts to end the war. But the latest diplomatic push seems to have produced no breakthrough.

Geopolitics.title: Photos: UN urges global aid after China, Nepal floods kill over 1,300
Geopolitics.summary: UN launches $50m appeal to aid over 84,000 flood survivors in Nepal amid cholera threat and sanitation challenges.

Geopolitics.title: Ethan Hawke receives the Deauville Talent Award
Geopolitics.summary: Known for starring in Dead Poets Society, the Before trilogy and Boyhood, Hollywood legend Ethan Hawke receives the #Deauville #Talent #Award in recognition of his career spanning nearly 40 years. He also plays the lead role in The Weight, screened at the Opening Ceremony of the 52nd Deauville #American #Film #Festival and due to be released in theaters on September 16. Our reporter Gaëlle Fonseca spoke to him on the red carpet.

Geopolitics.title: Trump again asks supreme court to restrict mail-in voting as midterms loom
Geopolitics.summary: Legal fight continues as states begin sending out ballots for voters to vote by mail in November’s midterm elections The Trump administration renewed its appeal to the US supreme court on Sunday to allow restrictions on mail-in voting, after a federal judge had blocked new limits on such ballots, just ahead of November’s midterm elections. The latest filing follows a decision by US district court judge Indira Talwani on Friday to extend a court order preventing the US Postal Service (USPS) from enforcing Donald Trump’s executive order. The Associated Press contributed reporting Continue readin

Geopolitics.title: The US now has access to more than half Australia’s military bases – could it drag the country unwillingly into war?
Geopolitics.summary: Exclusive: US-controlled weapons corporations and forces have control or access to more than 100 facilities across the continent, which some analysts describe as a ‘colonisation’ of Australia’s military. Find a map of them here US military presence in Australia, mapped – video Why can the US access so many Australian military bases? – podcast US military interests control or have access to more than 100 defence facilities on Australian soil, in what some analysts describe as a “saturation” – even a “colonisation” – of the Australian continent. Geopolitics.title: Commemoration held for late Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic
Geopolitics.summary: A commemoration was held Saturday in Belgrade for war criminal Ratko Mladic two days ahead of his burial, attended by dozens of former military personnel, family members and officials.

Geopolitics.title: Will Israelis re-elect Benjamin Netanyahu?
Geopolitics.summary: Recent opinion polls suggest opposition bloc is ahead of PM's coalition.

Geopolitics.title: Infantino to stand for re-election as FIFA president despite failed World Cup sell-off plan
Geopolitics.summary: FIFA President Gianni Infantino arrives to attend the opening game of the Women's U20 World Cup opening match between Poland and Argentina in Katowice, Poland, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026. (AP Photo/Beata Zawrzel) 2026-09-06T15:35:45Z MANCHESTER, England (AP) — FIFA President Gianni Infantino will stand for re-election, world soccer’s governing body said Sunday. Infantino has faced increasing pressure over his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup . Despite widespread calls for him to step down, FIFA said Infantino will seek next year to win a fourth and final term in office through 203

Geopolitics.title: Witkoff and Kushner call Kyiv talks 'substantive' after Moscow Putin meeting
Geopolitics.summary: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held meetings in Kyiv with Ukraine's President Zelenskyy on Sunday, a day after lengthy conversations with Russian President Putin in Moscow.

Science.title: 'Quiet' pulsar suddenly reveals three glitches in 15 years of observations
Science.summary: Using more than 15 years of observations from the Parkes radio telescope, astronomers detected three rotational glitches in the pulsar PSR J1637−4642—a young neutron star that had shown no signs of glitches since its discovery. The three glitches included one that changed its rotation rate by nearly 3 parts per million. Their paper was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 20. It has been accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Science.title: Advanced optical imaging reveals hidden activity in blood immune cells
Science.summary: A routine blood sample contains a diverse collection of immune cells that can reveal important clues about health and disease. These cells, known as peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), are widely used to study infections, autoimmune disorders, cancer and the immune system's response to treatment. Scientists typically identify these cells using fluorescent labels that attach to specific surface markers. While effective, those methods provide limited information about how the cells are functioning and can alter the cells during preparation. As reported in Biophotonics Discovery, a recent

Science.title: How much clearcutting can nature sustain? A study determines the ecological limit for boreal forest birds
Science.summary: A study led by the University of Jyväskylä in Finland evaluated, for the first time, an ecological threshold for the amount of clearcutting in boreal forests. According to the results, maintaining populations of bird species specialized in old-growth forests requires either a forest rotation period of at least 90 years on average or that approximately one-fifth of the forest area be excluded from clearcut management. The study provides a concrete target for the ecologically sustainable use of forests.

Science.title: Indonesia’s most dangerous fires are burning underground
Science.summary: Indonesia’s dangerous peat fires are surging early in the 2026 fire season as a strengthening El Niño and severe drought dry out wetlands that can burn underground for months. These slow smoldering fires are especially destructive because they release far more fine particles and several pollutants than typical tropical forest fires, while thick smoke can make them difficult for satellites to detect.

Science.title: Stunning Roman-era mosaic discovered in Turkey features 'Emerald' the cat and 'Ocean' the dog
Science.summary: A cat named Emerald and a dog named Ocean were memorialized in a Roman mosaic over 1,800 years ago.

Science.title: Six unusual structures identified at Earth's core-mantle boundary with the help of deep learning
Science.summary: Since scientists can't drill 2,900 km (1,800 miles) to the boundary between Earth's core and deep mantle, they must use information relayed by seismic waves recorded during earthquakes to study this region. In a new study published in the journal JGR Solid Earth, a group of scientists used deep learning to study a large set of a specific type of seismic wave. The analysis revealed six continuous bands of irregularities at the core-mantle boundary (CMB) that had previously appeared only as sparse patches.

Science.title: A mysterious signal around Earth could be dark matter
Science.summary: Scientists used Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere as a planet-sized detector to search for some of the lightest proposed forms of dark matter. The approach dramatically improved limits on ultralight axions and uncovered several intriguing dark photon signals that still need to be explained.

Science.title: SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches 27 Starlink satellites, lands on ship at sea (video)
Science.summary: SpaceX launched yet another batch of its Starlink internet satellites today (Sept. 6), sending them up from California's central coast.

Science.title: Scientists find a weak spot in one of the deadliest brain cancers
Science.summary: Researchers may have found a new way to weaken glioblastoma’s defenses against treatment. Blocking a protein called SET prevented tumors from forming in preclinical models, while targeting related proteins made cancer cells more vulnerable to radiation. The strategy works by restoring activity of PP2A, an enzyme that glioblastoma cells appear to suppress. Human testing will be needed to determine whether the approach is safe and effective.

Science.title: How bird movements are helping researchers track a global virus
Science.summary: While the highly virulent avian influenza strain has only recently been discovered on Australian shores, researchers at Deakin University have been working behind the scenes for years, anticipating what an outbreak might look like.

Science.title: 80,000-year-old “arrowheads” rewrite human history
Science.summary: Archaeologists have identified tiny 80,000-year-old projectile points in Uzbekistan that may have been used like arrowheads. Their size, design, and impact damage closely resemble weapons found much later at a Homo sapiens site in France. The discovery suggests sophisticated projectile technology may have appeared in Central Asia long before modern humans became firmly established in Europe, potentially rewriting a major chapter of human migration.

Science.title: Feel the Force with these 10 out-of-this-world Lego Star Wars starships
Science.summary: Whether you're a Jedi or a Sith, if you love Star Wars' iconic vessels you'll want to own these ten Lego Star Wars starships.

Science.title: Popular brain supplement linked to shorter lifespan in men
Science.summary: A large study involving more than 270,000 people has linked higher blood levels of the amino acid tyrosine to a shorter lifespan in men. Using both observational data and genetic analysis, researchers found that elevated tyrosine could potentially reduce male life expectancy by nearly a year, while no significant effect appeared in women. Tyrosine is found naturally in protein-rich foods and is also sold as a supplement for boosting focus and mental performance, making the finding especially intriguing.

Science.title: Growing up socially isolated linked to young people becoming NEET
Science.summary: About 1 million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training (NEET). The consequences for their health and income can be significant and long-lasting, with costs to the economy as well.

Science.title: AI can now control fusion plasma faster than humans can react
Science.summary: Princeton researchers have tested an AI system that can monitor and control fusion plasma in milliseconds, reacting far faster than a human operator. In one experiment, it predicted a damaging instability about 200 milliseconds before it appeared and adjusted the plasma to stop it from forming.

Science.title: Small molecular substitutions reshape energy pathways behind aggregation-induced emission
Science.summary: Certain chemical substances, broadly called luminogens, have an inherent ability to emit light. Most fluorescent molecules emit light in solution but lose their emission in the solid state, where the molecules aggregate.

Science.title: Germany's Isar Aerospace launches rocket into orbit from Norway
Science.summary: Germany's Isar Aerospace launched a rocket into orbit from Norway on Saturday as Europe races to boost its ability to economically send satellites into space independently of the United States.

Science.title: This “new” frog was hiding in plain sight for 100 years
Science.summary: A common frog found across Ecuador and Colombia has finally been recognized as its own species after more than a century of mistaken identity. Museum specimens from the 1800s helped scientists reveal that Pristimantis milpe had been hiding in plain sight all along.

Science.title: AI's water use is a problem, but shifting from electricity to solar or wind power could help
Science.summary: It depends. Though water consumption by data centers pales in comparison to that of some other industries, it's a problem in water-stressed regions. Water-saving cooling technologies could help.

Science.title: How small can a transistor get?
Science.summary: How small can a transistor actually get? And is smaller even still the goal?

Science.title: Extreme pressure turns blue pigment into record-long single-atom copper chains
Science.summary: As the electronics in our technology keep shrinking, traditional silicon-based chips are approaching their fundamental physical limits. Yet the wires connecting them might be able to shrink beyond conventional dimensions, as scientists have created one of the longest single-atom copper chains to date that could serve as molecular wires.

Science.title: 'Extreme' transistor can withstand heat of 1000-plus F — priming it for use in Venus-bound probes
Science.summary: The silicon carbide transistor is designed to avoid low controllability and current leakage, which typically become problems at high temperatures.

Science.title: The extinct American 'cheetah' was not a cheetah after all
Science.summary: With their slender bodies and long front legs, Miracinonyx trumani—often nicknamed the "American cheetah"—was long thought to be a North American analog of the African big cat. But in a new study published in the journal Current Biology, researchers reveal that the extinct cat was more closely related to pumas. Some populations living near the Arctic preyed almost exclusively on fish, challenging the long-held assumption that these "cheetahs" chased fast-running prey, such as pronghorns.

Science.title: Breaking through AlphaFold's limits to predict how proteins change shape
Science.summary: Conformational changes in proteins are vital to their function yet remain challenging for state-of-the-art artificial intelligence, such as AlphaFold3, to predict. Researchers at the Institute for Molecular Science (IMS), and the Graduate University for Advanced Studies, SOKENDAI introduced a repulsive force between predicted structures, allowing AlphaFold3 to sample the multiple conformational states that its default settings rarely capture.

Science.title: How algorithms are making our environments bland
Science.summary: The Pantone color of the year for 2026 is white. It's called Cloud Dancer, which is described as a "lofty white." This choice reflects a growing trend away from color in our visual world.

Science.title: NASA expands Deep Space Network with giant new dish in California desert
Science.summary: The new antenna will boost capacity on NASA's increasingly strained deep-space communications network as Artemis and other missions drive up demand.

Science.title: Ancient Egyptian tomb holding the king's 'keeper of secrets' unearthed at Saqqara
Science.summary: The tomb of a pyramid-age official has been found at Saqqara in Egypt.

Science.title: Haze emergency grips Malaysian Borneo town
Science.summary: Acrid smoke hung heavily over the Malaysian town of Serian, seeping into homes and cloaking roadside stalls, as residents navigated an air-quality emergency fueled by transboundary haze from Indonesia's raging fires.
